display_title: A potentially good inductive bias for learning SPNs, but whose significance and effectiveness is not clear

content.title: A potentially good inductive bias for learning SPNs, but whose significance and effectiveness is not clear
content.review:
##UPDATE 
I thank the authors for their answers and efforts in trying to improve the paper.
I believe the uploaded refactoring is becoming closer to being publishable and I encourage authors to iterate one more time over it. The points that still needs to be taken into account concern:
- removing references of FSPNs as 'new model' (starting from the title) and instead clearly say that they are proposing a new inductive bias that would be useful for learning
- amend the statements about the relationship of FSPNs and Bayesian Networks and SPNs 
- linking and contrasting FSPNs to other circuit models in a deeper way. In essence, what the authors are proposing is a k-way split operator which can still be represented with sum and product units (or decision nodes).
- report learning times and sizes of the learned circuits and competitors. It is not necessary to re-learn the best model for competitors but it is enough to report an average statistics over a resonable amount of trials/values in a grid search. 

## SUMMARY
The paper proposes a way to model and learn sum-product networks (SPNs) via multivariate split operations, which they call `factorize nodes`.
The authors claim that the resulting architecture -- called factorized SPN (FSPN) -- to be an hybrid of Bayesian networks and SPNs and being more tractable of the first while more expressive than the latter.
It seems to me that these, and numerous other claims, are not properly substantiated and this, jointly with a weak experimental evaluation, makes the paper in its current form immature for publication. Detailed comments below.


## PROS
+ Learning multivariate split nodes might be useful in practice

## CONS
- Novelty is limited, but more crucially, the true contribution is somehow hidden under several claims that  are unsubstantiated or imprecise 
- presentation will benefit from a major revision
- Relevant SPN variants are not cited (CSPNs, SPQNs) nor discussed in detail (SPGM)
- Experimental setting does not corroborate the empirical advantage of FSPNs


## NOVELTY and CORRECTNESS
While the underlying idea of introducing multivariate split nodes might provide an interesting inductive bias for learning SPNs, it value cannot be truly assessed from the current version of the manuscript.
First, claims about architectural novelty and increase expressiveness are not substantiated. Second, relevant literature implementing similar ideas is left out of the scope of the paper, either not properly discussed or experimented with.

In fact, FSPNs are still computational graphs that can be represented with sum and product node only, in essence, SPNs. This is evident from split nodes, which are just deterministic sum nodes -- ie only one sum node child is activated at a time [1]. The factorize node is indeed just another variant of split nodes with conditioning over multivariate events, and as such still representable with a deterministic sum, realizing the computations in page 5.

Note that multivariate split nodes have already been used in other kinds of circuits like PSDDs [2]. Conditioning in its more general form, has been introduced in SPNs with conditional SPNs (CSPNs) [3] and sum-product-quotient networks (SPQNs) [4].
These models should be compared with FSPNs, if not theoretically, at least empirically in some form.

Since this re-writing of split and factor nodes only increase the size of the underlying SPN polynomially (linearly) there is no gain in expressive efficiency. 
Moreover, this definitely does not increase expressiveness of SPNs, which already are universal representations. I suggest authors clarify the several claims about increased expressiveness by adopting the distinction between expressivenss and expressive efficiency by Martens and Melibani (more comments below on this).

It is true that FSPNs (and SPNs) are tractable whereas BNs might not, in general. However this holds from a representational perspective, and when it comes to learning, one can learn a BN that is tractable by design: e.g., either by compiling it into a circuit [5] or by bounding its treewidth [6].



A list of additional claims to be substantiated follows.

- "Sum-product network (SPN)’s performance significantly degrades in presence of highly correlated variables"
All in all, I believe one general confusion that permeates the paper raises when considering SPNs to be only/always learned with LearnSPN-like algorithms. As such they are deemed to be trees (not DAGs, hence less expressive efficient) and subject to the issues of a greedy algorithm that does not properly model correlations.

The job of sum nodes in SPNs is exactly to properly recover the correlations between sub-distributions encoded in the sub-circuits. Posing the whole circuit as a DAG clearly helps modeling more correlations in a more compact form than a tree.

- "PGMs tend to be much more interpretable and faster in inference." 
This is not true or at least misleading: PGMs include deep latent variable models and are in general intractable. Non-latent variable models might be deemed more interpretable in some cases (arguable).
  
-  "However, marginal probability inference on MRF is more difficult"
The hardness still comes from an integration/summation over an exponential number of states, as in BNs.

-  "SPNs can only accurately characterize the joint PDF of weakly correlated variables"
In Martens and Melibamini (2014), the argument is about expressive efficiency,  not expressiveness. Specifically they construct a precise distribution that cannot be compactly represented by any SPN. This distribution is not characterized by correlations alone, and moreover this does not imply that all fully connected models cannot be captured by SPNs.  

-  "As a result, the learned SPN becomes very deep and heavily overfitting, which may greatly degrade estimation accuracy"
Overfitting depends on the relationship of model and data complexity, expressive efficiency is more linked to a model class expressiveness per se. Again, I believe the focus here is on the limitations of LearnSPNs and not on SPNs as models per se.

-  "To the best of our knowledge, no existing class of PGM has so far addressed the trade-off between tractability and expressiveness in a truly satisfactory manner"
I agree with the authors that this is an open and interesting problem, however this problem has been addressed numerous time in the vast literature of tractable probabilistic models [7]. See also the references listed above.

-  "BN applies conditional factorization, which is accurate but difficult for inference.  SPN uses local independent factorization, which makes the model tractable but causes large errors in the presence of strongly correlated variables."
This claim is misleading, SPNs and other circuit representations exploit a finer form of conditional independence, context-specific independence [8], and if the distribution of a BN includes these independence statements, it might be compactly compiled in a circuit.


- "FSPN can compactly and accurately model the joint PDF of variables with any degree of dependence"
This statements need to be backed by some theory. To my understanding, since a factorization node is just a multivariate split node with $t$ children in an SPN, tractability depends on the value of $t$. Ultimately, this should be bounded by the treewidth of the distribution.


-  "Specifically, a sum node generates its children by splitting the data"
This sounds like a description of how learnSPN proceeds, I guess the authors want to talk about the generative model behind mixture models, which are encoded as sum nodes

- "However, when there exist strongly correlated variables in X,the product operation is unable to split them and SPN would repeatedly use the sum operation to splitD′into very small volumes, i.e.,|D′|=1in extreme"
Same as above


- "Without loss of generality, we can represent any event E in the probability space as a hyper-rectangle"

This is with loss of generality, events can be non-axis aligned polytopes. If that is the case computing their probabilities becomes hard for SPNs and therefore for FSPNs.


Some minor rewritings:

- "SPNs are PGMs"
To be pedantic they are not, the semantics behind these two graphical formalisms is quite different!

-  "While the probability inference time on an SPN is linear w.r.t. its node size"
"Circuit size", or "model size", or "number of nodes" are more appropriate

- "Therefore, MRFs are not suitable for probability inference tasks and thus mainly used for data generation and pattern recognition"
The application mentioned do use probabilistic inference underneath!

- "However,marginal probability inference for BN has a high time complexity and is sometimes even intractable."
Better to say is intractable in general, but sometimes tractable (e.g. for bounded treewidth)

-  "However, the learned BN structure maybe inaccurate, which in turn heavily degrades the probability estimation accuracy."
Sounds like a tautology!


## PRESENTATION
The paper is understandable, contains some typos and presentation might benefit a thorough proof-reading.

Among the typos, many involve calling model families with singular names, whereas plurals would be better. 
Some examples:
+ Probabilistic graphical model (PGM), a rich framework [...] aims -> Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs), a rich framework [...] aim
+ The most well-known PGM—Bayesian network (BN), -> The most well-known PGM—Bayesian networks (BNs),
+ BN applies [...] SPN uses -> BNs apply [...] SPNs use

Concerning notation, adopting a single way to denote splits and subsets of random variables for factorization nodes would improve readability (I have seen authors using S-H, X-H, W etc for the same case). 

- each value x of X−Hs
A bit confusing, why not i) using set difference operators (/) and ii) introducing a new set of variables `S = X \ H` with values `s`?

## EXPERIMENTS
Experimental results are not astonishing and fail to convince the reader on the adoption of FSPNs instead of other learners in the burgeoning literature of structure learning for SPNs. Moreover a comparison with relevant literature is missing.

Specifically, results reported in Table 2 show very minor gains and on 6 (on the seventh they are on par) datasets only wrt sota learners. Moreover, for these gains I suspect that a statistical test would deem the difference not that significant.
Concerning other competitors outperforming FSPNs, the authors claim 

"This is because they (SPN-BTB, ID-SPNs) use embedded BNs or MRFs in their structure to overcome thedrawbacks of SPN. However, such embedded components would result in slow inference speed."
This claim is misleading. First, the named competitors use BNs or MRFs only as leaf multivariate distributions over limited subsets of variables. These are compiled as circuits of the polysize and as such inference times are not supposed to degrade. 

To make a point in this regard, authors should report times for learning and inference of all models and show the sizes of the learned circuits (they do this in the Appendix for the synth exps only). 

Concerning synthetic experiments, authors use the RDC as a multivariate test for independence. This very same test is used for mixed SPNs (MSPNs) [9] for learning product and sum nodes, however MSPNs are left out of the comparison. Is there a particular reason why?
Overall, the effect of the different clustering and independence test algorithms used by the different competitors is not taken into account in this evaluation.

There is no clear ablation test on the use of different values for $t$ which clearly governs the size of the circuit.

Lastly, hyperparameters for the grid searches of all competitors are missing and reproducibility of the work is unclear.



### REFERENCES
[1] Darwiche, Adnan. Modeling and reasoning with Bayesian networks. Cambridge university press, 2009.

[2] Kisa, Doga, et al. "Probabilistic sentential decision diagrams." Proceedings of the 14th international conference on principles of 
knowledge representation and reasoning (KR). 2014.

[3] Shao, Xiaoting, et al. "Conditional sum-product networks: Imposing structure on deep probabilistic architectures." PGM 2020

[4] Sharir, Or, and Amnon Shashua. "Sum-product-quotient networks." International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2018.

[5] Lowd, Daniel, and Pedro Domingos. "Learning arithmetic circuits." (2012).

[6] Scanagatta, Mauro, et al. "Learning treewidth-bounded Bayesian networks with thousands of variables." Advances in neural information processing systems. 2016.

[7] Choi et al. "Probabilistic circuits: a unifying framework for tractable probabilistic models" 2020

[8] Boutillier et al., "Context-Specific Independence in Bayesian Networks" 2005

[9] Molina, Alejandro, et al. "Mixed sum-product networks: A deep architecture for hybrid domains." Thirty-second AAAI conference on artificial intelligence. 2018.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem III-3, 4, 5, 6)
content.comment:
Problem III-3: To make a point in this regard, authors should report times for learning and inference of all models and show the sizes of the learned circuits (they do this in the Appendix for the synth exps only).

Response:
Thank you for your comment. In the revision, we add the following experiments:
	1. On synthetic datasets, we add compassion with SPN-BTB, SPGM and BN-Tree. SPN-BTB is SPN with embedded BN as leaf nodes. SPGM is a hybrid model of SPN and BN. BN-Tree is a Chow-Liu tree.
	2. We provide the results of FSPN and all other models in terms of estimation errors and inference time in Section 6, Pages 8-9. An illustration is shown in Figure 2, Page 8. We provide the results of FSPN and all other models in terms of model size (and number of nodes) and training time in Appendix D. An illustration is shown in Figure 4 and Table 2 in Page 16.
	3. It is not informative to compare the inference time on benchmark real-world data since they only involve computing the log-likelihood of a data point. Even BN has a linear inference time w.r.t. its node size in such case.
	4. The benchmark testing on real-world datasets mainly aims at evaluating the model accuracy, which is highly related to the hyperparameters of the models. In our original paper, we perform a gird search on hyperparameters. However, as the search time is very long for some models on some datasets, we can not find the hyperparameters that reproduce their results. To remove the effects of hyperparameters, we quote results of other PGMs from their original paper in our revision. We think the original authors know how to find better hyperparameters of their models than us. Thus, we can’t report the model size and training time of the other models since we do not have their settings.

Problem III-4: Concerning synthetic experiments, authors use the RDC as a multivariate test for independence. This very same test is used for mixed SPNs (MSPNs) [9] for learning product and sum nodes, however MSPNs are left out of the comparison. Is there a particular reason why? Overall, the effect of the different clustering and independence test algorithms used by the different competitors is not taken into account in this evaluation.

Response:
Thank you for your comment. In fact, the SPN we compared in our original paper is MSPN. In our revision, we explicitly clarify this. We have tried different clustering and independence test algorithms of MSPN. The reported results is the best we can produce.

Problem III-5:  There is no clear ablation test on the use of different values for t which clearly governs the size of the circuit.

Response: 
We agree with you that t governs the size of the circuit. However, we cannot explicitly control the value of t because t refers to how many split nodes are needed to attain local independence between highly correlated variables and others. Therefore, our learning algorithm cannot explicitly decide t during its execution. We reserve the in-depth theoretical and empirical analysis of t in our future work.

Problem III-6: Lastly, hyperparameters for the grid searches of all competitors are missing and reproducibility of the work is unclear.

Response: 
  1.For the benchmark testing on real-world datasets, the results of other models in Table 1 in our revision are directly quoted from their original papers. We have explained the reason in our response to Problem III-3 (Point 4).
  2.For the synthetic datasets, we compare FSPN with other models. We run grid search of hyperparameters of all competitors using their original source codes from GitHub. 
  3.For our FSPN’s implementation and hyperparameters, we are cleaning the codes working on an open-source version upon publication.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem III Experiments-1, 2)
content.comment:
Problem III: Experiments.
Experimental setting does not corroborate the empirical advantage of FSPNs. Experimental results are not astonishing and fail to convince the reader on the adoption of FSPNs instead of other learners in the burgeoning literature of structure learning for SPNs. Moreover, a comparison with relevant literature is missing.

Response: 
According to your advice, we have the following revision:
	1. Add more experiments and analysis in comparison with other models on synthetic datasets. Please refer the details in our responses to Problem III-3, III-4.
	2. Correct our claims and update the results on the benchmark testing. Please refer the details in our responses to Problem III-1, III-2.
	3. Explain some concerns in our responses to Problem III-5, III-6.

Problem III-1: Specifically, results reported in Table 2 show very minor gains and on 6 (on the seventh they are on par) datasets only wrt sota learners. Moreover, for these gains I suspect that a statistical test would deem the difference not that significant. 

Response:
We agree with your comment. Our claim that “The performance SPGM, SPN-BTB and ID-SPN is slightly worse than FSPN” is not sufficiently supported by our experimental results. This claim is derived from the fact that SPGM and SPN-BTB achieve best performance on 5 and 6 datasets respectively, whereas FSPN achieve best performance on 7. However, we believe such difference might not be statistically significant. Therefore, in our revision, we change the claim to “The performance FSPN is comparable to SPGM, SPN-BTB and ID-SPN on the whole.”

Problem III-2: Concerning other competitors outperforming FSPNs, the authors claim "This is because they (SPN-BTB, ID-SPNs) use embedded BNs or MRFs in their structure to overcome the drawbacks of SPN. However, such embedded components would result in slow inference speed." This claim is misleading. First, the named competitors use BNs or MRFs only as leaf multivariate distributions over limited subsets of variables. These are compiled as circuits of the poly-size and as such inference times are not supposed to degrade.

Response:
First of all, we have removed this claim in our revision to avoid mis-understanding. We clarify that:
	1. The inference speed to compute the log-likelihood of a data point is not supposed to degrade on SPNs with embedded BNs or MRFs. Since our benchmark testing only consider computation of data points, so we remove our claim in the revision.
	2. The inference speed to compute the marginal probability of evidence, i.e., a range of data points, is supposed to degrade on SPNs with embedded BNs or MRFs as leafs, even with low tree-width. The reasons have been explained in our response to Problem I-4.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem I-13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19)
content.comment:
Problem I-13: "Specifically, a sum node generates its children by splitting the data" This sounds like a description of how learnSPN proceeds, I guess the authors want to talk about the generative model behind mixture models, which are encoded as sum nodes.
"However, when there exist strongly correlated variables in X, the product operation is unable to split them and SPN would repeatedly use the sum operation to split D′ into very small volumes, i.e., |D′|=1in extreme" Same as above

Response:
We agree with you that our original claims w.r.t. SPN are restricted to a particular type of SPN, tree-structured SPN which is learnt from LearnSPN type of structure learning algorithms. We apologize that we did not make this point clear in the original paper, which can be misleading. In our revised version, we have qualified all inaccurate or non-general points and discussed other SPN type that does not fall under such description. In details, we make the following revision:
	1. For the general description of SPN in the introduction part, Page 1, we revise the content to be “SPNs are recursively defined as weighted sums or products of smaller SPNs on simpler distributions. The most widely used SPN has a tree-structure, whose inference time is linear w.r.t. the number of nodes.”
	2. For the background review of SPN in Section 2, Page 3, we revise the content to be “Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) model the joint PDF by recursively applying two operations, namely sum and product, to split it into simpler PDFs to capture contextual independence. Specifically, a sum node represents a weighted sum of mixture models as…” We change our mis-claim that “a sum node splits data” to “a sum node represents a weighted sum of mixture models”.
	3. In Section 2, Page 3 on reviewing tree-structured SPNs, we revise the content to “However, tree-structured SPNs can not work well in presence of highly correlated variables in X.”

Problem I-14: "Without loss of generality, we can represent any event E in the probability space as a hyper-rectangle" This is with loss of generality, events can be non-axis aligned polytopes. If that is the case computing their probabilities becomes hard for SPNs and therefore for FSPNs.

Response:
Indeed, as the reviewer claimed, this is with loss of generality. We have removed the term “without loss of generality” and specified that we will consider hyper-rectangle type of queries in our revision. In the revised paper, we fix the claim to “We can represent E in a canonical form as a hyper-rectangle: …In this paper, we do not consider events with ranges that are not axis-aligned.”

Problem I-15: "SPNs are PGMs" To be pedantic they are not, the semantics behind these two graphical formalisms is quite different!

Response:
Thank you for your kindly review. Rigorously speaking, the semantics behind SPNs and PGMs are different. PGMs often refer to BNs or MRFs. However, broadly speaking, PGMs literally means probabilistic models with graphical structure, which is satisfied by SPNs and FSPNs. We are not the first to claim that SPNs are PGMs. In some literature work such as [Online Algorithms for Sum-Product Networks
with Continuous Variables, JMLR2016], they also claim in this way. In the international conference PGM, they also recognize SPNs as PGMs and have accepted a list of papers on SPNs. See the repo on https://github.com/arranger1044/awesome-spn. 

Problem I-16: "While the probability inference time on an SPN is linear w.r.t. its node size" "Circuit size", or "model size", or "number of nodes" are more appropriate

Response:
Thank you for your kindly review. In our revision, we use “number of nodes” to replace “node size”.

Problem I-17: "Therefore, MRFs are not suitable for probability inference tasks and thus mainly used for data generation and pattern recognition" The application mentioned do use probabilistic inference underneath!

Response:
Thank you for your kindly review. In our revision, we fix the claim to “Therefore, MRFs are not suitable for computing marginal probabilities and are thus mainly used for data generation and pattern recognition”.

Problem I-18: "However, marginal probability inference for BN has a high time complexity and is sometimes even intractable." Better to say is intractable in general, but sometimes tractable (e.g. for bounded treewidth)

Response:
Thank you for your kindly review. In our revision, we fix the claim to “However, although sometimes tractable, marginal probability inference on BNs is generally intractable.”

Problem I-19: "However, the learned BN structure maybe inaccurate, which in turn heavily degrades the probability estimation accuracy." Sounds like a tautology!

Response:
Thank you for your kindly review. In our revision, we fix the claim to “which may make the learned BN structure inaccurate for probability estimation.”

content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem I-9, 10, 11, 12)
content.comment:
Problem I-9: "As a result, the learned SPN becomes very deep and heavily overfitting, which may greatly degrade estimation accuracy" Overfitting depends on the relationship of model and data complexity, expressive efficiency is more linked to a model class expressiveness per se. Again, I believe the focus here is on the limitations of LearnSPNs and not on SPNs as models per se.

Response:
We agree with your statement. We have removed the statement on overfitting. What we want to claim is that if the SPN repeatedly splits the PDF into extreme smaller pieces, its estimation accuracy would be affected on the validation dataset. In our revision, we fix the statement to “However, tree-structured SPNs cannot work well in presence of highly correlated variables in X. …This large structure has low inference speed and poor generality, which degrades its estimation quality.” We actually state the limitations of tree-structured SPNs learned by LearnSPN types of algorithms. We have corrected this in our revision. See our response to Problem I-5.

Problem I-10: "To the best of our knowledge, no existing class of PGM has so far addressed the trade-off between tractability and expressiveness in a truly satisfactory manner" I agree with the authors that this is an open and interesting problem, however this problem has been addressed numerous time in the vast literature of tractable probabilistic models [7]. See also the references listed above.

Response:
This is a clear overclaim and we again apologize for not providing enough background review. We have changed this claim to “In summary, existing PGMs still have some drawbacks in terms of estimation accuracy or inference speed. Designing highly accurate and tractable PGMs remains a challenging task.” in the revision. We also add [7] and all references you mentioned into our reference list. We think our FSPN also make a meaningful exploration in the domain of tractable PGM.

Problem I-11: "BN applies conditional factorization, which is accurate but difficult for inference. SPN uses local independent factorization, which makes the model tractable but causes large errors in the presence of strongly correlated variables." This claim is misleading, SPNs and other circuit representations exploit a finer form of conditional independence, context-specific independence [8], and if the distribution of a BN includes these independence statements, it might be compactly compiled in a circuit.

Response:
We agree with you that such statement may induce a mis-understanding that SPN cannot capture conditional independence. However, it is not that case by the reasons you explained above. We do not mean SPN cannot capture conditional independence. We mean capturing such conditional independence for highly correlated variables is a hard task to tree-structured SPN learned by LearnSPN type of algorithms. In our revision, we fix claim to “BNs rely on conditional factorization, which is accurate but difficult for inference. Tree-structured SPNs use locally independent factorization, which cannot work well in presence of highly correlated variables.”

Problem I-12: "FSPN can compactly and accurately model the joint PDF of variables with any degree of dependence" This statement need to be backed by some theory. To my understanding, since a factorization node is just a multivariate split node with t children in an SPN, tractability depends on the value of t. Ultimately, this should be bounded by the treewidth of the distribution.

Response:
We agree with you that the tractability of FSPN depends on the value of t. The inference time complexity of FSPN can be represented as O(t^f * n), where f and n represents the number of factorize nodes and all nodes in FSPN. So far, in FSPN’s benchmark experiments and applications on query selectivity estimation, f is often a very small number near O(1), so the inference speed of FSPN is faster than BN and SPN. 

In fact, it is difficult to attain a desirable model in both theoretical and practical perspectives from the burgeoning stage, especially in the PGM domain. In order to theoretically ensure the tractability of FSPN, t needs to be bounded. We reserve this as a future work.

What we want to claim is that tree-structured SPNs’ expressive efficiency, but not expressiveness, in presence of highly correlated variables. In our revised paper, we fix this statement to “The most widely used SPN has a tree-structure, whose inference time is linear w.r.t. the number of nodes. content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem I-3, 4)
content.comment:
Problem I-3: Since this re-writing of split and factor nodes only increase the size of the underlying SPN polynomially (linearly) there is no gain in expressive efficiency. Moreover, this definitely does not increase expressiveness of SPNs, which already are universal representations. I suggest authors clarify the several claims about increased expressiveness by adopting the distinction between expressiveness and expressive efficiency by Martens and Melibani (more comments below on this).

Response:
Thank you for helping us understanding the difference between “expressiveness” and “expressive efficiency”. We have a mis-understanding on the concept of “expressiveness” in our original paper. We admit that our FSPN model does not increase expressiveness of SPN since they are all universal representations. 

We also agree that rewriting FSPN into DAG-structured SPN only increases the size polynomially and does not increase the expressive efficiency. However, for tree-structured SPN, this rewriting increases the size exponentially. As we replied in Problem I-1, each factorize node N could be regarded as a sum node whose children are all product nodes. Each product node’s left child is exactly the same as N’s left child. Each product node’s right child is a multi-leaf node modeling highly correlated variables in N’s right branch. Therefore, the left child may also contain factorize nodes. Thus, if we perform this rewriting recursively. The number of nodes of the resulting SPN is exponential w.r.t. the number of factorize nodes in FSPN. Therefore, for tree-structured SPNs learned by LearnSPN type of algorithms, FSPN has gain in terms of expressive efficiency. Specifically:
	1. In Section 2, Page 3, we review the drawbacks of tree-structured SPNs learned by LearnSPN type of algorithms. They do not identify highly correlated variables and would repeatedly split their joint PDFs, which results in large structure and low expressive efficiency. This is also claimed by Martens and Melibani in this paper.
	2. The above claim is supported by our experimental results in Section 6 and Appendix D on synthetic datasets. The model and node size of our FSPN is clearly smaller than SPNs.

Problem I-4: It is true that FSPNs (and SPNs) are tractable whereas BNs might not, in general. However, this holds from a representational perspective, and when it comes to learning, one can learn a BN that is tractable by design: e.g., either by compiling it into a circuit [5] or by bounding its treewidth [6].

Response:
We agree with this statement that BNs/MRFs with low tree-width or compiled into a circuit can have faster inference speed. However, such inference speed is relative. We analyze and verify this claim in the revised paper as follows:
	1. In Section 2, Page 3, we add the time complexity of probability inference on chow-liu tree as “On a Chow-Liu tree, inference time is O(n*d^(h+1)) where n, d and h represents the number of nodes, domain size and tree width, respectively. In our evaluation, the inference time on such BNs is still slow even when h = 1.” Therefore, the inference time cost is O(n*d^2) when h=1, which is not low.
	2. For a tree-structured SPN, its inference time is O(n) where n is the number of nodes in it. This time complexity requires that the marginal probability of any range could be computed in O(1) time on its leaf nodes. However, based on 1, the time complexity of using BN as leaf nodes, even with low tree-width, does not satisfy this requirement.
	3. By our evaluation in Section 6, Pages 8-9, we compare tree-structured SPN (marked as MSPN) and SPN with embedded BN leaf nodes (marked as SPN-BTB). The results in Figure 2, Page 8 shows that the inference speed of SPN-BTB is slower than MSPN.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem I-2(detailed part))
content.comment:
1. PSDD is a representation of probability distributions in the presence of logical constrains. Based on the original paper [2], PSDD is defined over binary variables, whereas FSPN can handle hybrid domains. If we are understanding it correctly, by “multivariate split nodes have already been used in PSDDs”, you are referring to the “decision node” defined in [2]. We agree with you that it is indeed multivariate split nodes. In addition, the “context” in PSDD, defined over a path of decision nodes of PSDD, can be viewed as the “region” in FSPN, defined over a path of split nodes. Indeed, they have quite similar utility. However, “decision node” is different from our split nodes for the following reasons. First, the variables under consideration of PSDD are binary, so each “split” of variable X is clearly defined in PSDD. However, split node in FSPN has to decide which value in the domain of X to split on. Algorithmically, split node is more complicated. We provide the details of our FSPN structure learning algorithm in Appendix C of the revised paper. Second, the original paper of PSDD did not propose any algorithm on structure learning and the existing PSDD structure learning algorithms do not seem to define a clear objective to learn decision node (this is based on our shallow understanding of PSDD, which might be incorrect). However, FSPN defines a clear objective to learn split node --- split on the domain of the weakly correlated conditional variables in order to achieve independence between highly and weakly correlated ones.
2. FSPN and CSPN have different objectives. CSPN is proposed to model Pr(Y|X). The inner nodes in CSPN are similar to SPN but its sum node is more general and more expressive. Each leaf node in CSPN can use deep neural network to models Pr(Yi|X) on a singleton variable Yi. CSPN harnesses the expressive power of neural network but it cannot be directly used to compute marginal probabilities because of the following reasons. As stated in the original paper, to represent marginal probability Pr(Y, X), one can learn an SPN on Pr(X) and a CSPN on Pr(Y|X) and use the direct dot product as Pr(Y, X). However, in the leaf node of CSPN, Pr(Y|X) is represented as Pr(Y|f(x)), where f can be neural network or other functions, which takes a data point x defined on the domain of X. Therefore, I suppose it is not possible to directly compute Pr(Y|X’) where X’ represents a range over domain of X instead of a data point x. In this case, it is not possible to directly infer the marginal probability such as Pr(0<Y1<1, Y2>3, 5<X2<7, X4>8), unless we sample data points from the range but the accuracy and inefficiency is unclear in this case. However, such probabilistic inference can be efficiently done in SPN or FSPN. Thus, I think CSPN and our proposed model FSPN are representing conditional distribution for different purposes. CSPN targets on making SPN’s expressiveness comparable to deep neural network in tasks such as image classification and image generation. However, FSPN targets on tasks like marginal (conditional) probabilistic inference. Moreover, we haven’t found any open source implementations for CSPN; thus, comparing with it empirically seems impossible.
3. The purposes of introducing conditional probability distribution are different for SPQN and FSPN. SPQN introduces a quotient node to represent Pr(Y|X) as the ratio Pr(Y, X)/Pr(X) where the two terms are modeled by two SPNs of this quotient node’s children (we cite this sentence for CSPN paper). Therefore, admittedly, the factorize node in FSPN, which decomposes Pr(Y, X) into Pr(Y|X) * Pr(X), can be realized by a SPQN’s product node with two children representing Pr(Y|X) and Pr(X). In theory, SPQN could subsume a FSPN but comes with a cost. As claimed in the original paper, the inference is only tractable when the condition variables of product node subsume the condition variables of all its children, which is not the case if it decomposes Pr(Y, X) into Pr(Y|X) and Pr(X). So again, SPQN and our FSPN have different objectives. The quotient node in SPQN is not used to ease the representation of Pr(Y, X). However, our FSPN introduce conditional distribution to simplify the representation of Pr(Y, X). Moreover, the original SPQN paper presents the theoretical foundation of SPQN but we haven’t found any algorithms on how to learn an SPQN in that paper or any other paper and there is no experiment on SPQN’s performance. Therefore, we don’t think we can compare with it empirically.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer3 (Problem I Novelty and Correctness-1, 2)
content.comment:
Problem I: Novelty and Correctness
While the underlying idea of introducing multivariate split nodes might provide an interesting inductive bias for learning SPNs, it value cannot be truly assessed from the current version of the manuscript. First, claims about architectural novelty and increase expressiveness are not substantiated. Second, relevant literature implementing similar ideas is left out of the scope of the paper, either not properly discussed or experimented with.

Response:
Thank you for your very helpful comments. We make the following revision:
	1. We correct our claims on the expressiveness and expressive efficiency of our FSPN and tree-structured SPNs. Please refer to the details in our responses to Problem I-1, I-3, I-5, I-8, I-9 and I-13
	2. We clarify our claims of our FSPN and BNs. Please refer to the details in our responses to Problem I-4, I-7, I-18 and I-19.
	3. We add comparison and discussion with models (PSDD, CSPN, SPQN) in both conceptual and empirical perspectives. Please refer to the details in our responses to Problem I-2.
	4. Some other concerns in our responses to Problem I-6, I-10, I-11, I-12, I-14, I-15, I-16 and I-17.

Problem I-1: In fact, FSPNs are still computational graphs that can be represented with sum and product node only, in essence, SPNs. This is evident from split nodes, which are just deterministic sum nodes -- ie only one sum node child is activated at a time [1]. The factorize node is indeed just another variant of split nodes with conditioning over multivariate events, and as such still representable with a deterministic sum, realizing the computations in page 5.

Response: 
We agree with your statement that a learned FSPN can be equivalently transformed into a SPN. The factorize node N could be regarded as a sum node whose children are all product nodes. Each product node’s left child is exactly the same as N’s left child. Each product node’s right child is a multi-leaf node modeling highly correlated variables in N’s right branch. 
If we could model such SPN as a tree, the inference cost on such a tree is the exactly same as our FSPN. However, to learn such a tree, one must consider the variables’ dependency degree and process them accordingly. Specifically, one must: 
  1.split the joint PDF into several regions such that in each region the highly correlated variables are local independent of the rest. 
  2.on each region, stop splitting the PDF of highly correlated variables and model them together as a multivariate leaf node. 
However, based on our current knowledge, existing SPN structure learning algorithms cannot realize both 1 and 2 since
  1.The learned sum node is not targeting at finding the local independence between highly correlated variables and others. It targets to find local independence between any possible variables, including independence across highly correlated variables.
  2.Even if it incidentally separates highly correlated variables with others, it may still try to split the joint PDF of highly correlated variables but do not stop, just as the drawbacks of the LearnSPN. 
Therefore, it is difficult to learn such a structure without taking variables’ dependency level into consideration in the learning process.

Problem I-2: Note that multivariate split nodes have already been used in other kinds of circuits like PSDDs [2]. Conditioning in its more general form, has been introduced in SPNs with conditional SPNs (CSPNs) [3] and sum-product-quotient networks (SPQNs) [4]. These models should be compared with FSPNs, if not theoretically, at least empirically in some form.

Response:
We agree with your statement and apologize for insufficient related-work discussion.
In the revised paper, we add discussion and comparison with PSDD, CSPN and SPQN as follows:
	1. In Section 2, Page 3, we review the main idea of the three models.
	2. In Section 3, Page 5, we compare our FSPN model with CSPN and SPQN conceptually. 
	3. In Section 6, Page 9, we compare our FSPN with PSDD on the benchmark data. 
	We made the following statement about PSDD, CSPN and SPQN, please correct us if it is imprecise. We believe that our proposed FSPN is different from these three models in terms of motivation, design choices and objectives. The details are as follows.

content.title: FSPN: A New Class of Probabilistic Graphical Model
content.review:
### Summary
The authors propose a framework to infer probabilistic graphical models in a general, fast and scalable framework, able to deal with highly correlated variables. The analysis on synthetic datasets show that the proposed method has high accuracy and fast inference.

### Reasons for score
I generally like the paper and the proposed approach. I found difficult to read the paper though, because of the formatting and in particular section , which is very mathematically dense.
Also, the authors in the analysis mention that "The performance SPGM, SPN-BTB and ID-SPN is slightly worse than FSPN" which goes against the results they showcase in the same page. It seems that especially SPGM and SPN-BTB are better than FSPN in at least 5 + 6 data sets (vs 7 of FSPN). The results suggest that such models are actually performing similarly. Also, 3 of the 6 data sets in which SPN-BTB is outperforming FSPN are the ones with the highest number of variables (with WebKB a close second, so almost 5). Also, is there a reason why SPN-BTB has not been used on 20 Newsgroups?

### Pros
- Generalises the PGM inference, with a scalable and fast approach
- Comprehensive analysis with state-of-the-art models on a wide range of data sets.

### Cons
- Paper presentation and clarity could be improved.
- Analysis is not always clear. Some claims do not seem to be supported by evidence.

### Minors
- Citations should be done using `\citep` command (they get confused with the text).
- "while overcomes" --> "while overcoming" page 2
- I don't believe the formatting is standard. The underlined paragraphs look wrong.

content.title: Multivariate factorization
content.review:
The paper proposes an extension of Sum Product Networks (SPNs), named factorize-sum-split-product networks (FSPNs), in order to achieve high expressiveness and tractability.

The proposed idea should be interesting, however the paper could be improved in many ways. 

It is not true that SPNs are recursively defined as weighted sums of smaller SPNs on data partitions, or products of smaller SPNs on independent variable subsets. This corresponds to the process of a specific algorithm learning the structure of a SPN. The definition of a SPN does not depend on the data neither on the variable independence. Even the description of SPNs at page 3 is strongly correlated to training data, that is not the case. Indeed, a sum node in an SPN does not split the data.

Furthermore, leaf node in an SPN could not represent a distribution of a single variable. It is possible to model a leaf node with a multivariate distribution.

Using a BN in an SPN does not increase the inference complexity if we have a BN with a low tree-width (1 for chow-liu trees).

It should be explained how the partitions are computed in order to obtain the ranges. Furthermore, how is chosen the split point? The use of EM for the split operation is unclear. 

The adopted split operation is not new. See for instance the Cutset-Networks, a kind of deterministic probabilistic circuit representing conditioning.

The authors say that in the experiment on synthetic data they adopted the pomegranate package for learning BNs. Currently, pomegranate only supports discrete Bayesian networks. The domain of the variables has not been defined in the paper. 

As regards the experimental evaluation on real-world dataset, the proposed approach seems to have the same performances on average when compared to SPN-BTB. Furthermore, the results for SPN-BTB reported in the original paper sometimes seem to be better than those reported in this paper.

Concluding, the paper address an interesting point, but in the current version is difficult to appreciate its contribution and novelty.

Problem 3: Using a BN in an SPN does not increase the inference complexity if we have a BN with a low tree-width (1 for chow-liu trees).

Response: 
Using a BN with a low tree-width can improves its inference speed, but it is still slow. We analyze and verify this claim in the revised paper as follows:
	1. In Section 2, Page 3, we add the time complexity of probability inference on chow-liu tree as “On a Chow-Liu tree, inference time is O(n*d^(h+1)) where n, d and h represents the number of nodes, domain size and tree width, respectively. In our evaluation, the inference time on such BNs is still slow even when h = 1.” Therefore, the inference time cost is O(n*d^2) when h=1, which is not low.
	2. For a tree-structured SPN, its inference time is O(n) where n is the number of nodes in it. This time complexity requires that the marginal probability of any range could be computed in O(1) time on its leaf nodes. However, based on 1, the time complexity of using BN as leaf nodes, even with low tree-width, does not satisfy this requirement.
	3. By our evaluation in Section 6, Pages 8-9, we compare tree-structured SPN (marked as MSPN) and SPN with embedded BN leaf nodes (marked as SPN-BTB). The results in Figure 2, Page 8 shows that the inference speed of SPN-BTB is slower than MSPN.

Problem 4: It should be explained how the partitions are computed in order to obtain the ranges. Furthermore, how is chosen the split point? The use of EM for the split operation is unclear.

Response:
In our revised paper, we add in Appendix C, Pages 14-15 to describe the details of the partition method. In fact, our FSPN structure learning algorithm is a general framework, which supports multiple partition method. We give two partition methods, namely Grid approximation of k-means and Greedy splitting. The Grid approximation of k-means cluster all data points into 2 parts by k-means. Then, we project the mid-point of the two clusters onto one dimension as the split point. The Greedy splitting chooses a value of a dimension as split point which largely break the correlations between variables. 

Problem 5: The adopted split operation is not new. See for instance the Cutset-Networks, a kind of deterministic probabilistic circuit representing conditioning.

Response:
We agree with you that adoption of split node is not new and looks similar to Cutset-Networks. As specified in the Cutset-Networks paper, it chooses a variable and create one branch for each of its possible values, which is space inefficient for large domains. The split node defined in our FSPN model has different roles:
	1. It splits the domain of the weakly correlated conditional variables into several RANGES, but not for each value.
	2. The split goal is to attain local independence between highly and weakly correlated variables. 
Several algorithms have been designed in Appdendix C to choose the split point.

Problem 6: The authors say that in the experiment on synthetic data they adopted the pomegranate package for learning BNs. Currently, pomegranate only supports discrete Bayesian networks. The domain of the variables has not been defined in the paper.

Responses:
In fact, our synthetic dataset only contains discrete variables. Many methods such as SPN-BTB also only support discrete domain. We clarify this in Section 6, Page 8 of our revised paper as “Each dataset contains 108 rows on 20 discrete variables with different domain size ranging from 5 to 100.”

Problem 7: As regards the experimental evaluation on real-world dataset, the proposed approach seems to have the same performances on average when compared to SPN-BTB. Furthermore, the results for SPN-BTB reported in the original paper sometimes seem to be better than those reported in this paper.

Response:
We agree that “the proposed approach seems to have the same performances on average when compared to SPN-BTB”. In the revised paper, we make the following changes:
	1. The difference on the number of SPN-BTB in our original paper and the SPN-BTB paper is due to the effects of hyperparameters. Although we perform a gird search, we may not use the same settings. To remove the effects of hyperparameters, we quote results of other PGMs from their original paper in our revision. We think the original authors know how to find better hyperparameters of their models than us.
	2. We believe the difference between SPN-BTB and our FSPN might not be statistically significant. Therefore, in our revision, we change the claim to “The performance FSPN is comparable to SPGM, SPN-BTB and ID-SPN on the whole.”

content.title: Re. inference complexity
content.comment:
If I'm understanding it correctly, you are referring to point-data query as complete evidence computing. We agree with you that in this case, every Bayesian network (not just tree BN) requires O(n) time complexity. However, when people discuss whether BN is tractable, they are referring to marginal inference. A point-data query is just a very special case in marginal probability inference.

For example, let's consider a BN modeling only two variables A, B. If the query is Pr(A=a, B=b), then this BN requires O(n) time complexity to compute it since it's just a product of two terms.
A more general form of complete evidence is Pr(A=Sa, B=Sb) where Sa, Sb is a subset of A, B's domain, respectively. Assume the BN has a tree structure with A parent to B.  Then Pr(A=Sa, B=Sb) = \sum_(a in Sa) \sum_(b in Sb) Pr(a) * Pr(b|a). The time complexity now is apparently O(n*d^2) where d is the maximum domain size.

In our synthetic dataset experiment, we are considering this more general formal of evidence so BN is significantly slower. For point-data query, the inference time makes little difference, so it is not very informative to compare this case.

Problem 2: Furthermore, leaf node in an SPN could not represent a distribution of a single variable. It is possible to model a leaf node with a multivariate distribution.

Response:
We agree with you that SPNs can be extended with multi-leaf node. Hence, we revise our paper as follows:
	1. We change the claim on SPN’s leaf nodes in Section 2, Page 3 to be “A leaf node COMMONLY maintains a univariate distribution …”.
	2. After that, in Section 2, Page 3, we review SPNs with multivariate leaf nodes. SPN-BTB and ID-SPN use embedded BNs or MRFs on multiple variables as leaf nodes in SPN.
	3. We discuss the difference of the multivariate leaf nodes in SPN-BTB/ID-SPN and the multi-leaf nodes used in our FSPN model. Please refer to Section 3, Page 5, the Third point of Comparison with other PGMs. Our multi-leaf nodes only model highly correlated attributes as their PDF can be modeled in a lower dimension space and can be compressed using dimension reduction, e.g. piecewise regression. Otherwise, if the correlations between variables is not high, the storage cost of multivariate leaf nodes grows exponentially. FSPN ensures multi-leaf nodes are only applied on highly correlated attributes, whereas SPN fails to guarantee that.
	4. In our evaluation (Section 6, Pages 8-9), we compare the performance of tree-structured SPN with univariate leaf nodes and SPNs with multivariate leaf nodes.

replying_to: Replying to FSPN: A New Class of Probabilistic Graphical Model

content.comment:
Thank you very much for your constructive reviews and helpful comments, which greatly improve our paper. According to your advices, we substantially revise our paper. It has been extended to 9 pages of main content and 16 pages with appendix. All revised contents are marked in blue color. 

We briefly summarize our revision as follows. For each reviewer, we give detailed responses to each problem you pointed out.

	1. We fix the claims on SPNs, BNs and our FSPN models to make our paper more rigorous. We correct our claims on the expressiveness and expressive efficiency of our FSPN and tree-structured SPNs. We correct some claims on the tractability of BNs. These claims emphasize our novelty and contribution.

	2. We add discussion and comparison with more related works, including Cutset network, PSDD, CSPN, SPQN and DAG-structured SPN. We conceptually clarify the difference of our FSPN model with them.

	3. We improve our presentation and readability by adding more descriptions on intuitive ideas, giving more implementation details, simplifying notations and presenting some examples.

	4. We add more experiments to evaluate our design choices of FSPN. We compare FSPN with more competitors on both synthetic and benchmark datasets. We fix some claims on the experimental results.

We hope the new version could better present our research. Thank you again for your work.
